title: Non-invasive tumor monitoring and diagnosis using deep learning
author: Yuan, Yan, et al.

steps.title: Activate environment and load libraries
steps.instruction: Activate the conda environment, start R, and load all required R packages.

steps.title: Load methylation matrices
steps.instruction: Clear the R workspace, load the pre‑processed DNA methylation matrices, and compute M‑values from beta‑values.

substeps.instruction: Load the objects: matrix_names, matrix_list, beta_matrix, group_sizes, group_names, groups, group_mapping.

steps.title: Plot beta‑ and M‑value densities
steps.instruction: Generate density plots for beta‑values and M‑values of the first 2,000 CpG sites and save the figures.

substeps.instruction: Select the first 2,000 rows: beta_subset <- beta_matrix[1:2000,]; M_subset <- M_matrix[1:2000,]
Call the custom function plot_methylation_density for each subset:
Inside the function, reshape data with rownames_to_column("cpg_id"), pivot_longer, merge with group_mapping, and plot density using ggplot2 with the following theme settings:
‑ legend at bottom, title centered, size 20 bold
‑ axis titles size 16, axis text size 14, legend text size 13, legend title removed
Save each plot with ggsave(filename, width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300).

steps.title: Plot mean‑variance relationships
steps.instruction: Create side‑by‑side scatter plots of mean versus variance for beta‑values and M‑values and export as a JPEG.

substeps.instruction: plot(mean_beta, var_beta, main = "", xlab = "Mean Beta-value", ylab = "Variance", pch = 16, cex = 0.8, col = "#8B000033")
plot(mean_M, var_M, main = "", xlab = "Mean M-value", ylab = "Variance", pch = 16, cex = 0.8, col = "#8B000033")

steps.title: Identify tumor‑specific DMPs
steps.instruction: Perform differential methylation analysis with limma to obtain the top 500 tumor‑specific differentially methylated positions (DMPs).

substeps.instruction: Create a design matrix that encodes group information (e.g., tumor, adjacent normal, healthy plasma).
Fit linear models to the M‑value matrix: fit <- lmFit(M_matrix, design); fit2 <- eBayes(fit).
Extract results for tumor vs. normal comparisons (tumor_results) and for tissue vs. plasma comparisons (tissue_results).
Define tissue‑specific non‑significant probes: tissue_not_sig_probes <- subset(tissue_results, adj.P.Val >= 0.05 | abs(logFC) < 0.2).
Select tumor‑significant probes: tumor_sig <- subset(tumor_results, adj.P.Val < 0.05 & abs(logFC) > 0.2).
Remove probes that are also tissue‑specific: tumor_sig <- tumor_sig[!rownames(tumor_sig) %in% tissue_not_sig_probes$probe_id, ].
Order by absolute logFC, keep the top 500: tumor_sig <- tumor_sig %>% arrange(desc(abs(logFC))) %>% slice_head(n = 500) %>% pull(probe_id).
Note: This filtering excludes sites that differ between adjacent normal tissue and normal plasma, retaining only tumor‑specific methylation sites.

steps.title: Generate heatmap of top DMPs
steps.instruction: Plot a heatmap of beta‑values for the 500 selected tumor‑specific CpG sites across all sample groups.

substeps.instruction: annotation_col <- data.frame(Group = group_mapping$group)  # column annotation for samples

steps.title: Save reference and test matrices
steps.instruction: Write the reference matrix and the two independent test matrices (AA‑sensitive and AA‑resistant) to tab‑separated files for downstream Oncoder analysis.

substeps.instruction: Critical note: The reference set contains 1,140 samples (484 prostate tumor + 656 healthy plasma). The test sets contain 74 AA‑sensitive and 107 AA‑resistant cfDNA methylation matrices. Ensure all files are in the working directory.

steps.title: Document beta and M value formulas
steps.instruction: Record the equations used to calculate beta‑values and M‑values for reference.

substeps.instruction: Beta‑value: Beta = M / (M + U + offset), where M = methylated intensity, U = unmethylated intensity, and offset is typically 100.

description: The detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) within cell-free DNA (cfDNA) has shown great potential for cancer diagnosis.2,3 However, a major hurdle in using ctDNA as a tumor biomarker is accurately distinguishing the minute fraction of ctDNA from vast background of cfDNA. DNA methylation profiling represents a promising strategy, as tumor-derived ctDNA typically exhibits methylation patterns distinct from those of background cfDNA.4 Moreover, DNA methylation profiling is characterized by high stability and broad genomic coverage, offering clear-cut advantages over other biomarkers, such as tumor-specific mutations and chromosomal aberrations.5,6,7,8,9 Here, we describe a protocol that uses Oncoder, an autoencoder-based framework, designed to automatically learn methylation patterns from a reference methylation atlas for predicting tumor fractions in plasma cfDNA. To demonstrate its utility, we leverage Oncoder to monitor the dynamics of tumor fraction in plasma cfDNA across 33 prostate cancer patients during abiraterone acetate (AA) therapy. As treatment with AA is known to largely eliminate non-resistant prostate cancer cells,10 this case study presents an illustrative biological scenario.
